## What Is an Employer of Record in Israel


An[Employer of Record (EOR)](https://www.bolto.com/blog/eor-definition-employer-of-record) is a third-party organization that becomes the legal employer of a worker in Israel on your behalf. You still direct day-to-day work, set compensation, and manage performance, while the EOR handles contracts, payroll, tax withholding, and statutory filings.


Israel’s employment framework makes this structure useful. Setting up your own entity generally means registering with the Israeli Registrar of Companies, opening a local tax file, and taking on ongoing obligations with Bituach Leumi, Israel’s National Insurance Institute, which covers social security contributions for every employee. That process takes time, and once running, it demands filings, renewals, and compliance checks that most foreign companies aren’t set up to manage alone.


An EOR skips that entity-building step. Instead of forming a subsidiary to hire one engineer in Tel Aviv, you work with a provider that already has the local legal structure in place. Bolto becomes the worker’s legal employer locally through its own entity, so you can hire in Israel within days instead of months. You keep control over the role. Bolto handles the legal employment layer underneath it.


## Employment Laws and Compliance Requirements in Israel


Hiring someone directly in Israel means taking on statutory obligations that go well beyond issuing a paycheck. Under Israeli labor law, employers generally owe pension contributions, National Insurance payments, severance accrual, and defined notice periods, and these typically apply from an employee’s first day.


Pension contributions are generally required under Israel’s pension law, combining employer and employee shares with severance-linked contributions. National Insurance, administered by[Bituach Leumi’s employer contributions program](https://www.btl.gov.il/English%20Homepage/Insurance/Employers/Pages/default.aspx) , funds benefits like unemployment and disability coverage, with employers generally remitting their share alongside the employee’s withheld portion.[Severance pay provisions](https://www.gov.il/en/pages/provisions-for-severance-pay) typically accrue monthly, even though they are often paid out only upon termination, and notice periods usually scale with tenure. Many sectors also operate under collective agreements that extend beyond the baseline labor code, adding sector-specific rules around wages, hours, and benefits that a foreign employer without the right[employer of record services](https://www.bolto.com/blog/employer-of-record-services-how-to-choose) can easily miss.

## EOR vs. Local Entity in Israel: Which Is Right for You


Choosing between an EOR and a local entity in Israel comes down to timeline, cost, and how long you plan to keep hiring there. An EOR makes sense when you need someone working quickly, want to test the market with one or two roles, or don’t yet have the in-house expertise to manage Bituach Leumi filings, pension contributions, and severance accrual on your own. A local entity starts to make more sense once your Israel headcount grows large enough that the fixed costs of registration, legal counsel, and ongoing compliance work are offset by lower per-employee costs at scale. For most companies just getting started, an EOR like Bolto is the faster, lower-cost route, as the comparison table above shows. A local entity still wins on long-term control over equity programs and direct IP ownership once the team is big enough to warrant it. If you’re unsure which path fits, weigh how many people you expect to hire in Israel over the next year against how much legal and administrative overhead you’re willing to take on now.


### Employer of Record (EOR): What It Does


An EOR lets you hire in Israel without any upfront entity commitment. Bolto takes on the legal employment relationship, so pension contributions, National Insurance, severance accrual, and benefits are handled as part of payroll from day one. You can bring someone on board in as little as 48 hours, and if the role doesn’t work out or your plans change, exiting is far simpler than winding down a subsidiary.


### Employer of Record (EOR): Where It Falls Short


An EOR works well for testing the market or hiring a handful of people, but it comes with tradeoffs once a team scales. Equity and benefits customization are more limited than what you’d design in-house, some structures restrict equity grants for workers hired through an EOR, and you’re relying on a vendor instead of your own HR infrastructure. For a large, long-term Israel team, the per-employee EOR fee can add up compared to the lower per-head cost of running your own entity at scale.


### Local Entity: What It Does


Setting up your own entity in Israel gives you full legal and HR control over the employment relationship. You own the IP directly, administer equity programs without EOR restrictions, and once your headcount is large enough, your cost per employee is typically lower than paying an ongoing EOR fee.


### Local Entity: Where It Falls Short


Entity setup generally takes weeks to months, and it comes with registration costs, local legal counsel, and ongoing accounting support that stay fixed whether you hire one person or ten. You also take on direct responsibility for Bituach Leumi filings, pension contributions, and severance accrual, and unwinding an entity is typically harder and costlier than ending an EOR relationship. This is general information, not legal advice, so consult a qualified employment lawyer before deciding how to structure your Israel entity.

Israel’s employment rules are detailed, but they don’t have to slow down your hiring plans. An employer of record gives you a way to bring on talent fast while keeping pensions, severance, and National Insurance filings handled correctly behind the scenes.
